claim: SARS-CoV-2 has caused nearly 2 million deaths
source: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic is an ongoing tragedy that has caused nearly 2 million deaths and massively disrupted the global economy.
evidence: Statement in introduction referencing pandemic statistics

claim: Most SARS-CoV-2 transmissions occur during the pre-symptomatic phase of infection
source: First, most transmissions occur during the pre-symptomatic phase of infection (He et al., 2020; Moghadas et al., 2020; Tindale et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The incubation period of SARS-CoV-2 often extends beyond an infected person's peak viral shedding
source: Underlying this observation is a highly variable incubation period, defined as time between infection and symptom onset, which often extends beyond an infected person's peak viral shedding (Ganyani et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: There is substantial over-dispersion of the secondary infection distribution for SARS-CoV-2
source: Second, there is substantial over-dispersion of the secondary infection distribution (individual R0) for an individual infected with SARS-CoV-2 (Endo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Most SARS-CoV-2 infected people do not transmit at all while a minority are super-spreaders
source: An over-dispersed R0 means that most infected people do not transmit at all (individual R0 = 0) while a minority of infected people are super-spreaders (individual R0 >5).
evidence: Explanation of over-dispersion concept in the context of SARS-CoV-2

claim: Approximately 10-20% of SARS-CoV-2 infected people account for 80% of transmissions
source: Overdispersion has been quantified: approximately 10–20% of infected people account for 80% of SARS-CoV-2 transmissions (Endo et al., 2020; Bi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: SARS-CoV-2 super-spreader events are well documented
source: SARS-CoV-2 super-spreader events, in which the duration of contact between a single transmitter and large number of secondarily infected people is often limited to hours, are well documented (Hamner et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Influenza has more homogeneous individual transmission than SARS-CoV-2
source: This pattern is not evident for influenza which has more homogeneous individual transmission (Cowling et al., 2009; Brugger and Althaus, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is often present intermittently in the upper airways for many weeks
source: SARS-CoV-2 is often present intermittently in the upper airways for many weeks (Qi et al., 2020; Cao et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Influenza is rarely shed for more than a week
source: while influenza is rarely shed for more than a week (Pawelek et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Viral load is recognized as a strong determinant of transmission risk
source: Viral load is recognized as a strong determinant of transmission risk (Watanabe et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: For influenza, the dose of viral exposure is related to the probability of infection in human challenge studies
source: For influenza, the dose of viral exposure is related to the probability of infection in human challenge studies (Memoli et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Early antiviral treatment reduces household transmission of influenza
source: and early antiviral treatment reduces household transmission (Pebody et al., 2011; Goldstein et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Viral exposure dose determines likelihood of SARS-CoV-1 infection in mice
source: Studies in mice definitively demonstrated that viral exposure dose determines likelihood of SARS-CoV-1 infection, (Watanabe et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: SARS-CoV-2 experiments in golden hamsters are highly suggestive of dose-dependent infection
source: and SARS-CoV-2 experiments in golden hamsters are also highly suggestive of dose-dependent infection (Sia et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Reduction of genital herpes simplex virus-2 shedding with antiviral treatments decreases probability of transmission
source: Reduction of genital herpes simplex virus-2 shedding with antiviral treatments decreases probability of transmission (Corey et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Suppressive antiretroviral therapy for HIV virtually eliminates the possibility of partner-to-partner sexual transmission
source: Suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV virtually eliminates the possibility of partner-to-partner sexual transmission and has limited community transmission dramatically (Rodger et al., 2019; Cohen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The within-host mathematical model captures observed upper airway viral kinetics from 25 people from four different countries
source: Briefly, the model captures observed upper airway viral kinetics from 25 people from four different countries (Wölfel et al., 2020; Lescure et al., 2020; Young et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: Model is fit to data from cited studies

claim: The model captures an early viral peak followed by a decelerating viral clearance phase, a temporary plateau at a lower viral load, and rapid viral elimination
source: Key observed features include an early viral peak followed by a decelerating viral clearance phase, which in turn leads to a temporary plateau at a lower viral load, ultimately followed by rapid viral elimination.
evidence: Description of model output matching observed data patterns

claim: Only half of study participants provided longitudinal viral load data from the very early days of infection
source: One limitation of our model is that only half of study participants provided longitudinal viral load data from the very early days of infection when COVID-19 is often pre-symptomatic.

claim: The mean incubation period for SARS-CoV-2 is 5.2 days
source: where the mean incubation for SARS-CoV-2 is 5.2 days compared to 2 days for influenza (Ganyani et al., 2020; Cowling et al., 2009; Lauer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The mean incubation period for influenza is 2 days
source: where the mean incubation for SARS-CoV-2 is 5.2 days compared to 2 days for influenza (Ganyani et al., 2020; Cowling et al., 2009; Lauer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The model captures that ~75% of 10,000 simulated transmitters do not infect any other people
source: Despite assuming that each infected person sheds at a high viral load for a period of time (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), the model captured the fact that ~75% of 10,000 simulated transmitters do not infect any other people and that each increase in the number of individual transmissions is associated with a lower probability (Figure 2a).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 2a

claim: ~10% of all infected people and ~35% of all transmitters are super-spreaders (defined as producing at least five secondary infections)
source: If super-spreaders are defined as those who produce at least five secondary infections, we estimate that ~10% of all infected people and ~35% of all transmitters are super-spreaders.

claim: ~6% of all infected people and ~25% of all transmitters are super-spreaders (defined as producing at least 10 secondary infections)
source: If super-spreaders are defined as those who produce at least 10 secondary infections, we estimate that ~6% of all infected people and ~25% of all transmitters are super-spreaders.

claim: ~2.5% of all infected people and ~10% of all transmitters are super-spreaders (defined as producing at least 20 secondary infections)
source: If super-spreaders are defined as those who produce at least 20 secondary infections, we estimate that ~2.5% of all infected people and ~10% of all transmitters are super-spreaders.

claim: Super-spreaders producing ≥5 secondary infections contribute to ~85% of all secondary infections
source: If super-spreaders are defined as those producing ≥5, ≥10, or ≥20 secondary infections, the contribution to all secondary infections is estimated at ~85%, ~70%, or ~44%, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Table 1

claim: The model recapitulated the high variance of the serial interval observed within SARS-CoV-2 transmission pairs, including negative values
source: The model also recapitulated the high variance of the serial interval observed within SARS-CoV-2 transmission pairs, including negative values observed in the data (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: Model fitting results shown in Figure 2c,d

claim: The mean serial interval (4.4 days) provides an accurate approximation of mean generation time for SARS-CoV-2
source: We next projected generation time, defined as the period between when an individual becomes infected and when they transmit the virus, for all transmission pairs and identified that the mean serial interval (4.4 days) provides an accurate approximation of mean generation time.

claim: The variance of generation time was considerably lower than serial interval variance for SARS-CoV-2
source: However, the variance of generation time was considerably lower and by definition does not include negative values.

claim: The optimized ID curve for SARS-CoV-2 has an ID50 of 10^7 viral RNA copies
source: The optimized ID curve has an ID50 of 107 viral RNA copies and a moderately steep slope (Figure 3a).
evidence: Model fitting results shown in Figure 3a

claim: The TD50 for SARS-CoV-2 was slightly higher at 10^7.5 viral RNA copies
source: The TD50 for SARS-CoV-2 was slightly higher at 107.5 viral RNA copies (Figure 3a).
evidence: Model fitting results shown in Figure 3a

claim: Transmission is very unlikely (~0.00005%) given an exposure to an infected person with an upper airway viral load of <10^4 SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies
source: To assess the impact of these parameters on transmission, we performed simulations with 10,000 transmitters and concluded that transmission is very unlikely (~0.00005%) given an exposure to an infected person with an upper airway viral load of <104 SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies

claim: Transmission is unlikely (~0.002%) given an exposure to an infected person with a viral load of <10^5 SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies
source: and unlikely (~0.002%) given an exposure to an infected person with a viral load of <105 SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies.

claim: Transmission is much more likely (39%) given an exposure to an infected person who is shedding >10^7 SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies
source: On the other hand, transmission is much more likely (39%) given an exposure to an infected person who is shedding >107 SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies

claim: Transmission is 75% likely given an exposure to an infected person with a viral load of >10^8 SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies
source: and 75% given an exposure to an infected person with a viral load of >108 SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies.

claim: Infected persons are likely to be most infectious for a ~0.5-1.0 day period between days 2 and 6 after infection
source: In general, infected persons are likely to be most infectious (i.e., above TD50) for a ~0.5–1.0 day period between days 2 and 6 after infection.

claim: The observed wide variance in serial interval results primarily from the possibility of highly discrepant incubation periods between the transmitter and infected person
source: We therefore conclude that the observed wide variance in serial interval (Figure 2c) results primarily from the possibility of highly discrepant incubation periods between the transmitter and infected person, rather than wide variability in shedding patterns across transmitters.

claim: The solved value for exposed contact network heterogeneity (ρ) is 40
source: The solved value for exposed contact network heterogeneity (ρ) is 40 indicating high variability in day-to-day exposure contact rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d) with an average number of exposed contacts per day (θ = 4).

claim: The average number of exposed contacts per day (θ) is 4
source: The solved value for exposed contact network heterogeneity (ρ) is 40 indicating high variability in day-to-day exposure contact rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d) with an average number of exposed contacts per day (θ = 4).

claim: Super-spreader events require viral load exceeding 10^7 SARS CoV-2 RNA copies and a high number of exposure contacts
source: We generated a heat map from our TD curve to identify conditions required for super-spreader events which included viral load exceeding 107 SARS CoV-2 RNA copies and a high number of exposure contacts on that day.

claim: There is an inflection point between 10^6 and 10^7 SARS CoV-2 RNA copies, after which large increases in the number of daily exposure contacts prominently increases the number of transmissions
source: We observed an inflection point between 106 and 107 SARS CoV-2 RNA copies, after which large increases in the number of daily exposure contacts prominently increases the number of transmissions from a single person (Figure 4a).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 4a

claim: Over 50% of simulated secondary infections were associated with a transmitter who has a high number of exposed contacts (11-100 per day) and a viral load exceeding 10^6 RNA copies
source: We next identified that over 50% of simulated secondary infections were associated with a transmitter who has a high number of exposed contacts (11–100 per day) and a viral load exceeding 106 RNA copies (Figure 4c)
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 4c

claim: The serial interval was longer during the initial stages of the pandemic in Wuhan (before January 22, 2020)
source: The serial interval was reported to be longer during the initial stages of the pandemic in Wuhan (before January 22, 2020, termed as pre-lockdown) possibly because infected people were initially less likely to self-isolate after developing symptoms (Li et al., 2020; Ali et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The optimized ID curve during the early phase of the pandemic (pre-lockdown) has an ID50 of 10^5 viral RNA copies, ~100-fold lower than post-lockdown
source: Importantly, the optimized ID curve has an ID50 of 105 viral RNA copies during the early phase of the pandemic (pre-lockdown), ~100-fold lower than post-lockdown (Figure 3a).
evidence: Model fitting results comparing pre- and post-lockdown periods

claim: ID50 estimates from pre-lockdown reflect more prolonged and intimate exposure contacts that were of higher risk given an equivalent viral load
source: Keeping in mind that ID50 is an average measure, we propose that ID50 estimates leading to more prolonged and intimate exposure contacts that were of higher risk given an equivalent viral load, whereas estimates from later in the pandemic (Figure 3) reflect greater social distancing and higher use of masking.

claim: ID50 values for influenza were lower than SARS-CoV-2
source: ID50 values for influenza were lower than SARS-CoV-2, but a direct comparison cannot be made because tissue culture infectious dose (TCID) has been more commonly used for measurements of influenza viral load, whereas viral RNA is used for SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: Comparison of model fitting results with caveat about measurement differences

claim: The model captures that 40% of influenza infected people do not transmit to anyone else
source: The model captures the fact that 40% of people in this influenza infected cohort do not transmit to anyone else and that each increase in the number of individual transmissions is associated with a lower probability (Figure 6a).
evidence: Model fitting results shown in Figure 6a

claim: Super-spreader events involving five or more people were ~5-fold less common overall for influenza relative to SARS-CoV-2
source: In keeping with the observed data, our model simulations predicted that relative to SARS-CoV-2, super-spreader events involving five or more people were ~5-fold less common overall and 10-fold less common among transmitters (~2% of all infected people and ~3% of transmitters) (Figure 6b, Table 1).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 6b and Table 1

claim: Influenza super-spreaders defined as those infecting ≥5 individuals contributed to only ~10% to all transmissions
source: Super-spreaders defined as those infecting ≥5 individuals contributed to only ~10% to all transmissions (Table 1).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Table 1

claim: The TD50 for influenza was 10^6.1 TCID/mL
source: The TD50 for influenza was 106.1 TCID/mL.

claim: For influenza, infected persons were likely to be most infectious for a ~0.5-1.0 day period
source: In general, infected persons were likely to be most infectious (i.e., above TD50) for a ~ 0.5–1.0 day period.

claim: The observed low variance in serial interval for influenza primarily results from the low variance in incubation period
source: The observed low variance in serial interval (Figure 6c) primarily results from the low variance in incubation period (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b) and the limited variability in timing of peak viral loads across transmitters.

claim: The influenza contact network never resulted in days with more than 15 exposure contacts per day
source: The contact network never resulted in days with more than 15 exposure contacts per day, which severely limited the possible number of transmissions from a single person relative to SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 8a, Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 8a

claim: For influenza, secondary transmissions to fewer than five people accounted for 90% of infections
source: Secondary transmissions to fewer than five people accounted for 90% of infections (Table 1)
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Table 1

claim: For influenza, over 50% of infections were associated with a transmitter who had fewer than 10 exposure contacts per day and a viral load exceeding 10^4.5 TCID
source: We next identified that over 50% of infections were associated with a transmitter who had fewer than 10 exposure contacts per day and a viral load exceeding 104.5 TCID (Figure 8c)
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 8c

claim: The median per contact transmission risk among simulated transmitters was slightly higher for influenza than SARS-CoV-2
source: The median per contact transmission risk among simulated transmitters was slightly higher for influenza; however, the upper bounds of 75% and 95% percentile of transmission risks among simulated transmitters were marginally higher for SARS-CoV-2 compared to influenza along with a longer tail of low transmission risk beyond 7 days after exposure (Figure 9a).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 9a

claim: The transmission risk was considerably higher for the 25% of simulated SARS-CoV-2 infections with the highest viral loads
source: The transmission risk was considerably higher for the 25% of simulated SARS-CoV-2 infections with the highest viral loads, suggesting that a substantial subset of infected people may be more pre-disposed to super-spreading.

claim: For SARS-CoV-2, median time above ID10 was 2.7 [0, 7] days
source: For SARS-CoV-2 and influenza, median [range] time above ID10 was 2.7 [0, 7] and 2.4 [1.6, 3.7] days, respectively

claim: For influenza, median time above ID10 was 2.4 [1.6, 3.7] days
source: For SARS-CoV-2 and influenza, median [range] time above ID10 was 2.7 [0, 7] and 2.4 [1.6, 3.7] days, respectively

claim: For SARS-CoV-2, median time above TD50 was 0 [0, 0.5] days
source: For SARS-CoV-2 and influenza, median [range] time above TD10 was 1.4 [0, 2.5] and 1.2 [0, 2.0] days, respectively; median time above TD25 was 0.8 [0, 1.3] and 0.3 [0, 1.3] days, respectively; median time above TD50 was 0 [0, 0.5] and 0 [0, 0.4] days, respectively

claim: For influenza, median time above TD50 was 0 [0, 0.4] days
source: For SARS-CoV-2 and influenza, median [range] time above TD10 was 1.4 [0, 2.5] and 1.2 [0, 2.0] days, respectively; median time above TD25 was 0.8 [0, 1.3] and 0.3 [0, 1.3] days, respectively; median time above TD50 was 0 [0, 0.5] and 0 [0, 0.4] days, respectively

claim: Predicted distributions of serial interval and generation time were unchanged by shifts in the exposed contact network
source: Under all scenarios, predicted distributions of serial interval (Figure 9g, Figure 9—figure supplement 1) and generation time (Figure 9h, Figure 9—figure supplement 1) were unchanged by shifts in the exposed contact network.
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 9g,h and Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: Despite differing viral shedding kinetics, the kinetics of infectivity are extremely similar between influenza and SARS-CoV-2
source: In summary, we conclude that despite differing viral shedding kinetics (Figure 10a, top), the kinetics of infectivity are extremely similar between influenza and SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 10a, bottom).
evidence: Conclusion from model simulation results shown in Figure 10a

claim: Over-dispersed contact networks, likely due to wider airborne dispersal of virus in equivalent crowded environments, explain the ability of SARS-CoV-2 to initiate super-spreader events
source: Over-dispersed contact networks, likely due to wider airborne dispersal of virus in equivalent crowded environments, explain the ability of SARS-CoV-2 to initiate super-spreader events (Figure 10b).
evidence: Conclusion from model simulation results shown in Figure 10b

claim: An approximately 40% decrease in the average exposed contact rate lowered R0 below 1
source: An approximately 40% decrease in the average exposed contact rate lowered R0 below 1 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1a

claim: Limiting exposure contacts to no more than five per day is nearly equivalent to limiting exposure contacts altogether
source: We identified that limiting exposure contacts to no more than five per day is nearly equivalent to limiting exposure contacts altogether and that only a small decrease in mean exposure contact rate can achieve R0 < 1 if exposure events with more than 20 contacts are eliminated (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Model simulation results shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2

claim: 62% of simulated transmissions occurred in the pre-symptomatic phase for SARS-CoV-2, compared to 10% for influenza
source: Much of the highest transmission risk for SARS-CoV-2 exists in the pre-symptomatic phase (Figure 9b) which explains why 62% of simulated transmissions occurred in the pre-symptomatic phase for SARS-CoV-2, compared to 10% for influenza.

claim: 62% of SARS-CoV-2 super-spreader events with secondary transmissions ≥5 fell exclusively in the pre-symptomatic period
source: Similarly, 62% and 21% of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza super-spreader events with secondary transmissions ≥ 5, and 39% of SARS-CoV-2 super-spreader events with secondary transmissions ≥ 10 fell exclusively in the pre-symptomatic period.

claim: 21% of influenza super-spreader events with secondary transmissions ≥5 fell exclusively in the pre-symptomatic period
source: Similarly, 62% and 21% of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza super-spreader events with secondary transmissions ≥ 5, and 39% of SARS-CoV-2 super-spreader events with secondary transmissions ≥ 10 fell exclusively in the pre-symptomatic period.

claim: The model provides a transmission dose response curve which specifies that a nasal viral load below ~10^4 RNA copies is unlikely to result in transmission
source: Our model provides a plausible link between SARS-CoV-2 shedding kinetics and the virus' most fundamental epidemiologic properties. First, we identify a transmission dose response curve which specifies that a nasal viral load below a certain threshold (conservatively ~104 RNA copies) is unlikely to result in transmission – consistent with the overall rarity of positive cultures at these levels (van Kampen, 2020).

claim: The model predicts a relatively steep TD curve such that transmission becomes much more likely when a susceptible person contacts an infected person shedding above 10^8 viral RNA copies
source: We also predict a relatively steep TD curve such that transmission becomes much more likely when a susceptible person contacts an infected person shedding above 108 viral RNA copies.

claim: The simulated relationship between viral RNA and probability of positive viral culture qualitatively matches the dose response observed in formal dose challenge experiments performed with SARS-CoV-1 in mice
source: The amount of viral RNA can be roughly converted to the probability of a positive viral culture which approximates infectiousness, and this simulated relationship qualitatively matches the dose response observed in formal dose challenge experiments performed with SARS-CoV-1 in mice (Watanabe et al., 2010).
evidence: Model results compared to cited experimental data

claim: The model predicts a short period—averaging less than two days—of high transmission risk for SARS-CoV-2
source: While the duration of shedding for SARS-CoV-2 is often three weeks or longer, (Qi et al., 2020; Cao et al., 2020) our model predicts a short period—averaging less than two days—of high transmission risk.

claim: The high-risk window increases to 2-3 days when fit to pre-lockdown conditions in Wuhan
source: We note that our model was fit to pandemic settings where self-isolation upon development of symptoms was normative, and this high-risk window increases to 2–3 days when fit to pre-lockdown conditions in Wuhan.

claim: The duration of infectivity for SARS-CoV-2 is predicted to be comparable to that of influenza
source: This duration of infectivity is predicted to be comparable to that of influenza.

claim: The model predicts that transmission after the first week of infection is quite rare
source: Our model predicts that transmission after the first week of infection is quite rare.

claim: The observed high heterogeneity in serial interval is attributable almost entirely to the variable nature of the incubation period
source: The observed high heterogeneity in serial interval is attributable almost entirely to the variable nature of the incubation period, rather than transmission occurring extremely late after infection.

claim: The range of SARS-CoV-2 serial intervals is much wider than the range of generation times
source: While our estimate for mean generation time is equivalent to that of mean serial interval, it is notable that the range of SARS-CoV-2 serial intervals is much wider than the range of generation times.

claim: A low nasal viral load, particularly during late infection, may not require full patient isolation procedures in the absence of aerosolizing procedures
source: Our model suggests that a low nasal viral load, particularly during late infection, may not require full patient isolation procedures in the absence of aerosolizing procedures.
evidence: Inference from model results with caveat

claim: Time since first positive test may be predictive of lack of contagion
source: Our results also suggest that time since first positive test may be predictive of lack of contagion, although more viral load kinetic studies will be needed to confirm the existing observation that viral loads after a week of infection are usually low and associated with negative viral cultures (van Kampen, 2020).
evidence: Inference from model results with supporting citation

claim: SARS-CoV-2 super-spreading events are dependent on a large number of exposure contacts during the relatively narrow 1-2 days peak infectivity window
source: Another finding is that SARS-CoV-2 super-spreading events are dependent on a large number of exposure contacts during the relatively narrow 1–2 days peak infectivity window.

claim: Super-spreader potential may be a signature property of infection, rather than a characteristic of a tiny subset of infected people
source: Because we predict that super-spreader potential may be a signature property of infection, rather than a characteristic of a tiny subset of infected people, this result also has practical implications.

claim: Newly diagnosed people within small clusters may be past the peak of their super-spreading potential
source: Our results demonstrate that newly diagnosed people within small clusters may be past the peak of their super-spreading potential.

claim: Influenza infection is much less predisposed to super-spreader events than SARS-CoV-2
source: Influenza infection is much less predisposed to super-spreader events than SARS-CoV-2.

claim: Influenza shedding at levels above those required for a high probability of transmission occurs with only slightly lower frequency than SARS-CoV-2
source: Yet, influenza shedding at levels above those required for a high probability of transmission occurs with only slightly lower frequency.

claim: Viral kinetics are unlikely to drive the markedly different probability of super-spreader events between SARS-CoV-2 and influenza
source: Therefore, viral kinetics are unlikely to drive the markedly different probability of super-spreader events between the two viruses—despite the fact that the overall duration of SARS-CoV-2 shedding exceeds duration of influenza shedding often by more than 2 weeks.

claim: The exposure contact networks of SARS-CoV-2 transmitters are highly dispersed relative to those of influenza
source: Rather, our analysis suggests that the exposure contact networks of SARS-CoV-2 transmitters are highly dispersed relative to those of influenza.

claim: The most likely explanation underlying differing exposure contact networks is that SARS-CoV-2 is more predisposed to airborne transmission than influenza
source: The most likely explanation underlying differing exposure contact networks is that SARS-CoV-2 is more predisposed to airborne transmission than influenza (van Doremalen et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference from model results with supporting citation

claim: A SARS-CoV-2-infected person in a crowded poorly ventilated room will generate more exposure contacts than an influenza infected person in the exact same room
source: Our result suggests that a SARS-CoV-2-infected person in a crowded poorly ventilated room will generate more exposure contacts than an influenza infected person in the exact same room, likely based on wider dispersal and / or longer airborne survival of the virus.

claim: A much higher proportion of SARS-CoV-2-infected people than influenza infected people do not transmit at all
source: On the other hand, a much higher proportion of SARS-CoV-2-infected people than influenza infected people do not transmit at all.

claim: High viral load shedding in the pre-symptomatic phase may be defined by lack of cough or sneeze leading to limited spatial diffusion of virus
source: One theoretical explanation is that high viral load shedding in the pre-symptomatic phase is defined by lack of cough or sneeze leading to limited spatial diffusion of virus.

claim: It is possible that a proportion of infected people never shed virus at high enough viral loads to allow efficient transmission
source: Alternatively, it is also possible that a proportion of infected people never shed virus at high enough viral loads to allow efficient transmission.

claim: The model was fit to viral RNA and viral culture for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza, respectively
source: Second, based on the quality of available data, we fit our models for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza to viral RNA and viral culture, respectively.

claim: Data during early SARS-CoV-2 infection is fairly limited
source: Third, data during early SARS-CoV-2 infection is fairly limited such that we may be underestimating variance of initial viral growth rates.

claim: The intra-host model of SARS-CoV-2 was fit to heterogeneous data from different continents and with different sampling techniques and PCR assays
source: Fourth, our intra-host model of SARS-CoV-2 was fit to heterogeneous data from different continents and with different sampling techniques and PCR assays (Goyal et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of model fitting approach with citation

claim: R0 estimates for SARS-CoV-2 have varied temporally and spatially across the globe
source: Similarly, R0 estimates for SARS-CoV-2 have varied temporally and spatially across the globe and the same is likely true for influenza.
evidence: Statement about variability in epidemiological data

claim: Social interaction matrices are very likely to differ among countries and between urban and rural areas
source: Social interaction matrices are very likely to differ among countries and between urban and rural areas.
evidence: Statement about variability in social contact patterns

claim: Estimates of TD50 are necessarily imprecise based on available data and should serve only as a conservative benchmark
source: For these reasons, our estimates of TD50 are necessarily imprecise based on available data and should serve only as a conservative benchmark.

claim: Differing aerosolization properties of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza underly the observed overdispersion of individual R0 for SARS-CoV-2 relative to influenza
source: Nevertheless, we are confident that differing aerosolization properties of the two viruses underly the observed overdispersion of individual R0 for SARS-CoV-2 relative to influenza, regardless of geographic location.

claim: Super-spreader events are a globally generalizable feature of SARS-CoV-2 epidemiology
source: Nevertheless, it is extremely clear that super-spreader events are a globally generalizable feature of SARS-CoV-2 epidemiology.

claim: Fundamental epidemiologic features of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza infections can be directly related to viral shedding patterns in the upper airway as well as the nature of exposure contact networks
source: In conclusion, fundamental epidemiologic features of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza infections can be directly related to viral shedding patterns in the upper airway as well as the nature of exposure contact networks.
